According to DeSmet and colleagues (2016), participatory design represents stakeholder involvement in two distinct ways: as informants who provide input and feedback, or as co-designers who act as equal partners [2]. This framework highlights that while co-design involves collaboration, it may not always carry the same political or empowerment-driven weight as traditional participatory design. sections.text: To function as a safe storage platform, peer-to-peer systems must effectively protect data against temporary unavailability and the disruptive effects of peer churn [4]. The high prevalence of peer departures necessitates that these systems constantly generate new replicas to maintain high durability levels [1]. While P2P storage networks offer data redundancy that ensures uninterrupted access even when peers become unavailable, this reliability is not automatic [3]. Traditional approaches have primarily focused on the placement of redundant objects at random peers or at peers determined by a Distributed Hash Table (DHT) name-space [2]. However, few existing systems are capable of selecting the optimal replication rate that balances replication cost against durability, such as minimizing costs without threatening the target durability level [1].

sections.title: Evaluation of Redundancy Techniques
sections.text: A 2007 study evaluated and compared various redundancy techniques for P2P storage based on availability, accessibility, and maintainability [4]. This research provided specific quantitative results regarding the performance of different redundancy schemes, measured by a metric referred to as Stretch. The study reported a Stretch value of 2.00 for one specific redundancy scheme configuration. Further analysis within the same paper yielded a Stretch value of 3.00 for another configuration. The evaluation also identified a configuration with a Stretch value of 4.00. Additionally, the paper documented a result with a Stretch value of 6.00. In contrast, other configurations demonstrated lower Stretch values, including 1.43 and 1.72. These varying Stretch values illustrate the significant differences in performance and reliability characteristics among different redundancy strategies.

sections.title: The AutoProc Optimization Method
sections.text: To address the challenge of balancing cost and durability, a 2011 paper proposed a method called AutoProc [1]. This method is designed to select the right replication rate, thereby balancing replication cost and durability effectively [1]. The system operates through a continuous monitoring and estimation process. First, a monitor component periodically collects peer failure information [1]. Based on this collected data, an estimator obtains the parameters needed by the controller and assigner [1]. These parameters include the peer permanent failure rate and the historical failure distribution [1]. The AutoProc framework utilizes a durability approximation formula to configure the system appropriately. Furthermore, it employs a replication rate threshold equation to determine the necessary configuration settings. By integrating these components, AutoProc aims to minimize replication costs while ensuring that the durability target is not compromised [1].

Another project, Ivy, is a writeable P2P storage system [3]. In Ivy, each participant maintains a set of logs that record modifications made to the system [3]. sections.title: Taxonomy of Detection Approaches
sections.text: Research in this domain categorizes business process anomaly detection into three primary families: statistical methods, process mining techniques, and machine learning algorithms [1]. While these categories are distinct, they often overlap in their application to event log analysis. The choice of approach depends on whether the goal is to identify deviations from a known model, detect statistical outliers, or uncover semantic inconsistencies in process behavior.

sections.title: Process Mining and Conformance Checking
sections.text: A standard workflow in process mining involves using discovery methods to construct process models from event logs, which are then subjected to conformance checking to identify anomalous traces [1]. This technique specifically detects deviations between the constructed process model and the actual process executions [1]. By utilizing these models, process mining provides the foundational basis for comparing current executions against an existing reference model or another event log [3]. Beyond simple conformance, various specialized process mining methods are applied to investigate event logs, including dotted-chart analysis, social network miners, and originator-by-task matrices [2][2][2]. These tools help visualize and quantify different aspects of process behavior to support anomaly identification.

sections.text: Machine learning techniques, such as Support Vector Machines, are employed to mine rules that must be strictly met by a process to avoid being classified as anomalous [4]. An alternative strategy focuses on detecting rules that, when met, identify anomalous behavior; this approach utilizes explorative process mining by experts to generate a labeled training set for the detection model [4]. Additionally, some approaches incorporate ontologies to gain additional domain knowledge about the processes under analysis, enhancing the context available for detection [4]. These methods often rely on supervised or semi-supervised learning paradigms to define what constitutes normal versus abnormal behavior.

sections.title: Core Task Definitions and Operational Requirements
sections.text: Person-following behavior is fundamentally composed of two distinct but interconnected challenges: robot navigation and person tracking [2]. To execute this behavior effectively, a robot follower must perform a specific sequence of tasks, which includes finding the specified person, following that person, avoiding obstacles, and resuming tracking after an occlusion event [1]. These requirements establish the baseline for any system designed to operate in dynamic environments where human subjects may move unpredictably or be temporarily hidden from view [1].

sections.title: Strategic Planning for Re-identification
sections.text: Beyond the immediate capabilities of robust person detection and tracking, person-following robots must possess the ability to plan for re-identification when necessary [3]. This strategic planning is critical because simple tracking algorithms may fail when the target is obscured, requiring the robot to proactively determine how to regain visual contact [3]. The necessity for such planning highlights that the system must not only react to the current state of the environment but also anticipate potential loss of the target and prepare a recovery strategy [3].

sections.text: Despite the theoretical frameworks for person following, practical application has been limited by the lack of affordable and powerful sensors as well as efficient person-tracking techniques [2]. While robot navigation itself has been extensively investigated, the specific challenge of person following remains constrained by these hardware and software deficiencies [2]. The absence of cost-effective sensing solutions and optimized tracking algorithms has hindered the widespread deployment of these systems in real-world scenarios [2].

sections.title: Navigation Strategies Under Clear Visibility
sections.text: In scenarios where no occlusion occurs, the robot typically navigates to a predefined person-following position, which is often a fixed location behind the target [4]. This navigation is achieved using a model predictive controller (MPC), which enables the robot to maintain a consistent following distance and trajectory [4]. The use of MPC allows for simultaneous person-following and obstacle avoidance by continuously adjusting the robot's path based on the target's movement [4].

sections.text: When an occlusion event occurs, the robot shifts its strategy to leverage available perception information to locate and navigate to the best position for re-finding the target person [4]. By utilizing perception data to determine the optimal vantage point, the robot can effectively resume tracking once the target becomes visible again [4].

sections.text: The peer review process is fundamental to maintaining the quality of scientific publications [2]. However, the rapid increase in submissions to top-tier venues in machine learning and natural language processing has created an excessive burden on human reviewers [2]. This surge in volume raises concerns that the overload may compromise the quality of the reviews themselves [2]. Furthermore, there is a gap in coverage, as not all research areas and sub-areas currently possess a comprehensive, up-to-date review [1]. These factors collectively motivate the development of automated systems to assist or replace manual review generation.

sections.title: Early Methodological Approaches
